foodDescription: Flaky, diamond-shaped pastries filled with ricotta or mushy peas, sold hot from pastizzerias for well under a euro. Malta’s everyday snack, eaten at any hour.
A round, chewy, sourdough flatbread split and filled with tomato, tuna, olives, capers, and onion. UNESCO listed the bread and its culture in 2020.
Rabbit stewed in wine and garlic, often eaten as two courses: the sauce over spaghetti first, then the meat. Considered the national dish.
A light, garlicky fish soup with tomato, rice, and plenty of mint and marjoram. Fishermen’s food, especially good in Marsaxlokk.
A pie of lampuki, the dolphin fish that runs past Malta in autumn, baked with spinach, olives, and capers in pastry.
A thick dip of mashed broad beans with garlic, chili, and herbs, eaten with crackers or bread. Once sold from carts in the street.
Maltese bread rubbed with tomato and drizzled with olive oil, topped with tuna, capers, olives, and onion. A simple summer lunch.
Little round sheep’s milk cheeses from Gozo, eaten fresh, dried, or peppered and cured. Found on most Maltese platters.
Diamond-shaped pastries filled with dates and aniseed, deep-fried and sold hot from stalls, especially at the Valletta ferry and village feasts.
Rings of pastry filled with a dark, spiced treacle mixed with citrus. A Christmas sweet now sold year-round.
Malta’s own soft drink since 1952, made from bitter oranges and herbs. Bittersweet, like a soda version of an aperitif.
Malta’s best-known beer, brewed since the 1920s by the Farsons brewery. Cold and easy, and on tap in every bar.
